title: CFA Economics: Aggregate demand and aggregate supply (AD/AS)
subtitle: The framework for answering: will this shock push up inflation, or push up unemployment?
openingQuestion: World oil prices spike. Under the AD/AS model, what happens to output and the price level in an oil-importing economy?
openingOptions: Both output and the price level rise, since higher costs force firms to charge more
Short-run aggregate supply shifts left: prices rise, output falls
Both output and the price level fall, because households cut their spending
Nothing changes, since the oil price only touches the energy sector itself
explanation: An oil price spike is an adverse supply shock. It raises production costs right across the economy and pushes the short-run aggregate supply curve (SRAS) to the left. The result is a higher price level alongside lower output - stagflation, the most awkward situation a central bank can face, because its two objectives of price stability and full employment now point in opposite directions.

realWorldExample.company: The 1973 oil crisis and the inflation of 2022
realWorldExample.description: The 1973 OPEC embargo quadrupled the oil price and produced stagflation across the developed world - double-digit inflation alongside rising unemployment, which the prevailing models had held to be impossible. 2022 replayed a milder version as energy and food prices surged, forcing central banks to choose between containing inflation and protecting growth.

quiz.question: Which factor shifts the AGGREGATE DEMAND (AD) curve to the right?
options: A large rise in the number of workers joining the market
A sharp global fall in the price of input raw materials
An improvement in the economy's labour productivity
Higher public spending, tax cuts, monetary easing
quiz.explanation: AD = C + I + G + (X - M). Anything that raises consumption, investment, government spending or net exports pushes AD to the right. The other three answers - input costs, productivity, the size of the labour force - all act on the SUPPLY side and shift AS, not AD. Cheaper raw materials lower production costs; more workers and better productivity raise the economy's capacity to produce. Mistaking a supply factor for a demand factor is the single commonest error on exam questions of this type.

quiz.question: Why is the LONG-RUN aggregate supply curve (LRAS) drawn vertical?
options: Because potential output depends only on the real resource base
Because prices in the long run are permanently fixed
Because long-run demand always equals long-run supply
Because the central bank holds inflation at its stated target
quiz.explanation: LRAS is vertical at potential output because in the long run both prices and wages adjust freely. The output an economy can sustainably produce is set purely by real factors: the quantity and quality of labour, the capital stock, the level of technology. Prices are not fixed in the long run - the opposite, they are fully flexible, which is what makes the curve vertical. Printing money or raising aggregate demand only lifts the price level; it does not raise potential output. This is the foundation of long-run monetary neutrality.

quiz.question: The economy has real output BELOW potential output. What is that called, and what does it imply for policy?
options: An inflationary gap, which argues for tightening policy
A recessionary gap, which argues for easing policy
Long-run equilibrium, so no intervention is needed
Stagflation, which needs both kinds of policy at once
quiz.explanation: Real output below potential is a recessionary gap, also called a negative output gap. Resources are underused, unemployment sits above its natural rate, and inflationary pressure is weak - so this is not long-run equilibrium, which by definition sits at potential. The standard policy response is to stimulate demand: cut rates, raise public spending, or cut taxes. The inflationary gap is the mirror image, where real output exceeds potential, the economy overheats and tightening is called for.

quiz.question: Why does stagflation put a central bank in a far harder position than a demand shock?
options: Because the central bank has no authority to intervene in commodity prices
Because a supply shock cannot be measured by any statistical indicator at all
Because fighting inflation and fighting a fall in output pull in opposite directions
Because cost-push inflation always lasts longer than demand-pull inflation
quiz.explanation: A demand shock moves prices and output in the same direction, so one policy direction addresses both. A supply shock moves them in opposite directions: tighten to bring inflation down and output falls further; ease to protect output and inflation rises further. Central banks never set commodity prices under either kind of shock, so that is not what changed. Supply shocks are perfectly measurable in the data. And how long cost-push inflation persists depends on expectations, not on a rule.

quiz.question: What does stimulating aggregate demand when the economy is already at potential output produce in the long run?
options: Real output stays permanently above the original level of potential output
A higher price level, with real output back at its original potential
Neither the price level nor real output changes from before the stimulus
Potential output rises automatically by exactly the size of the stimulus
quiz.explanation: The long-run aggregate supply curve is vertical at potential output, which labour, capital and technology determine. Stimulus shifts only the demand curve, so in the long run all of it passes into prices - the foundation of long-run monetary neutrality. Output does rise in the short run, so it is not true that nothing changes; it simply does not stay there. And spending cannot raise potential output, which is a supply-side quantity.

keyTakeaways: AD = C + I + G + (X - M); anything acting on spending shifts AD, anything acting on costs or productive capacity shifts AS
An adverse supply shock pushes SRAS left: prices rise and output falls at the same time - stagflation
LRAS is vertical at potential output: in the long run aggregate demand sets only the price level, not output
A recessionary gap argues for easing; an inflationary gap argues for tightening

practicePrompt.question: The government launches a large stimulus package while the economy is already at potential output. Under AD/AS, what follows in the short run and the long run?
options: Output rises sustainably in both horizons, since extra spending always creates growth
Short run output above potential; long run back to it but with higher prices
No effect at all, because the economy is already at full employment
The price level falls as the stimulus draws out extra supply of goods
practicePrompt.explanation: Stimulus at full employment creates an inflationary gap: in the short run output exceeds potential because resources are being worked beyond their sustainable rate, but the tight labour market pushes wages up, production costs rise, and SRAS shifts left until output returns to potential. The long-run outcome is the same output at a higher price level - inflation with no real growth to show for it.

summary.keyIdea: AD/AS is the framework for reading any economic shock: work out whether it hits demand or supply, then infer the direction of output and the price level.
summary.commonMistake: Mistaking a supply factor for a demand factor - for instance thinking cheaper raw materials shift AD, when they shift AS
summary.action: For every macro headline, ask yourself: is this a demand shock or a supply shock, and which curve does it move which way?

application.title: Applying this in CFA analysis
application.message: AD/AS connects straight to asset pricing: a demand shock moves inflation and growth together (good for cyclical equities), while a supply shock moves them apart (bad for equities and bonds alike).
application.secondary: It is why the traditional 60/40 portfolio performs so poorly through a stagflation - both asset classes take the hit at once.

sections.text: The AD/AS model is the framework for the question every investor has to answer: will the shock that just happened push inflation up, push growth down, or both?

AD = C + I + G + (X - M): household consumption, business investment, government spending, and net exports. The AD curve slopes down for three reasons: a lower price level raises real wealth so people spend more (the wealth effect), lowers the real interest rate so investment rises (the interest rate effect), and makes domestic goods relatively cheaper than foreign ones so exports rise (the real exchange rate effect).
Aggregate supply: short run versus long run

items: SRAS (short run) slopes up: wages and some input prices are sticky in the short run, so a higher output price widens margins and firms produce more
LRAS (long run) is vertical at potential output: every price has adjusted, so output depends only on labour, capital and technology
What shifts SRAS: input prices, nominal wages, inflation expectations, business taxes and subsidies
What shifts LRAS: the size of the labour force, capital accumulation, technological progress, institutional quality

sections.text: A favourable demand shock (AD shifts right): output up, prices up - the economy heats up. An adverse demand shock (AD shifts left): output down, prices down - recession with disinflation. A favourable supply shock (SRAS shifts right, say cheap energy or a productivity gain): output up, prices down - the ideal case. An adverse supply shock (SRAS shifts left): output down, prices up - stagflation. Only in the two demand cases do the goals of price stability and output stability point the same way; under a supply shock the central bank is forced to choose.

sections.label: Watch for this in the CFA exam
sections.text: AD/AS questions almost always take the same form: given an event, which way do output and the price level move. The three-step drill: (1) does the event hit demand or supply, (2) does that curve shift left or right, (3) read off the new intersection. Do not skip step 1.

diagram.label: Aggregate demand = consumption + investment + public spending + net exports
Short-run aggregate supply slopes up, long-run is vertical
Demand shock: output and prices move together
Supply shock: output and prices move apart
Infer whether the shock pushes up inflation or unemployment
